options.text: Because Objective-C lacks support for multithreading primitives.

options.explanation: Right. Locking all view properties creates heavy synchronization overhead.

options.text: Because Apple chips only have a single physical CPU core.
options.explanation: Apple silicon chips feature multiple performance and efficiency cores.

options.text: Because iOS apps are restricted from creating background threads.

options.text: Swift converts the sync call into an async call with a compiler warning.

questions.prompt: Why must all user interface updates run on the main thread in iOS? Answer in 2 to 4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that UI frameworks like UIKit are not thread-safe to avoid synchronization overhead.
Mentions that screen redraws must synchronize with hardware refresh rates (60Hz or 120Hz).
Notes that modifying views from background threads causes data races and corrupted layouts.

questions.modelAnswer: UI updates must run on the main thread because UI frameworks like UIKit are intentionally not thread-safe. Adding locks to every view property would hurt rendering performance and drain battery. In addition, view layouts and Core Animation commits must synchronize with the display refresh rate of 60 or 120 hertz.

questions.prompt: What happens when the main thread is blocked by heavy synchronous work, and what user experience issues result? Answer in 2 to 4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that blocking the main thread prevents the run loop from processing touches and drawing frames.
Describes user-facing issues like frozen interfaces, dropped frames (hitches), and stuttering animations.
Mentions that prolonged blocking leads to an OS watchdog crash.

questions.modelAnswer: When heavy synchronous work runs on the main thread, the main run loop cannot process user touch events or draw new display frames. This causes the user interface to freeze, creating dropped frames and stuttering animations known as hitches. If the main thread stays unresponsive for too long, the operating system kills the app.

questions.prompt: Describe the iOS watchdog timer and identify the exception code generated when it terminates an app. Answer in 2 to 4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that the iOS watchdog monitors app responsiveness and kills processes that block the main thread.
Identifies the crash exception code 0x8badf00d.
Notes that timeouts are typically ~5 seconds at launch and ~10 seconds during runtime.

questions.modelAnswer: The iOS watchdog is an operating system process that monitors application responsiveness. If an app blocks its main thread for roughly ten seconds during runtime or five seconds at launch, the watchdog terminates the process. The crash log records the exception code `0x8badf00d`, which indicates that the application failed to keep its main thread responsive.

questions.prompt: Why does calling `DispatchQueue.main.sync` from the main thread cause an immediate deadlock? Answer in 2 to 4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that calling sync pauses the current thread until the submitted closure completes.
Explains that the submitted closure cannot execute because the main thread is blocked waiting.
States that the mutual wait creates an unrecoverable freeze.

questions.modelAnswer: Calling `DispatchQueue.main.sync` from the main thread causes an immediate deadlock because `sync` pauses the main thread until the closure completes. However, because the main queue is serial and the main thread is paused, the closure can never start running. Both the thread and the queue wait for each other indefinitely.

questions.prompt: How does `@MainActor` in Swift provide compile-time safety for user interface code? Answer in 2 to 4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that @MainActor is a global actor binding types or methods to the main thread.
Explains that the Swift compiler prevents background threads from mutating main actor state directly.
Mentions that cross-actor access requires asynchronous await calls.

questions.modelAnswer: `@MainActor` is a global actor that binds classes, structs, or functions strictly to the main thread. The Swift compiler checks actor isolation at compile time and prevents background threads from mutating UI state directly. Accessing `@MainActor` members from other contexts requires an asynchronous `await` call, eliminating data races before the code runs.
